parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the four diodes around R in Fig. 7.1 and recall what a diode does to current direction. Compare the input $V_{IN}$ type with the output $V_{OUT}$ type in Fig. 7.2.
Hint 2: Think about what happens to the negative half-cycles of the sinusoidal input. Are they blocked or are they flipped to become positive?
parts.proper_answer: The circuit provides full-wave rectification of the input voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the diode bridge**
You have an a.c. sinusoidal input $V_{IN}$ that keeps changing direction, but the output in Fig. 7.2 is always positive. The four diodes form a bridge. A diode conducts in one direction only, so the bridge automatically steers current through R in the same direction on both halves of the input cycle.

Step 2: **Name the process**
Changing a.c. to unidirectional pulsating d.c. is called rectification. Because both the positive and the negative half-cycles of $V_{IN}$ appear as positive pulses at the output, with no gaps missing, it is full-wave rectification, not half-wave.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: power in resistor P = V^2 / R
hints: Hint 1: Maximum power must occur at the maximum voltage. Read the peak value of $V_{OUT}$ carefully from the top of the pulses in Fig. 7.2.
Hint 2: Recall how electrical power in a resistor links voltage and resistance, then substitute $R = 370 \, \Omega$ and your peak voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the peak voltage**
Power in a resistor is largest when voltage is largest. From Fig. 7.2 the tops of all the $V_{OUT}$ pulses reach $$V_{MAX} = 9.0 \text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Apply power law**
For a resistor, Joule heating gives $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ Use the peak voltage for peak power: $$P_{MAX} = \frac{(9.0)^2}{370} = \frac{81}{370} \approx 0.219 \text{ W} \approx 0.22 \text{ W}$$ This confirms the stated value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how $P$ depends on $V_{OUT}$. When $V_{OUT}$ is zero, what must $P$ be, and when $V_{OUT}$ is maximum, what must $P$ be?
Hint 2: Compare the timing of the zeros and peaks in Fig. 7.2 with what you need in Fig. 7.3. Should the period change?
Hint 3: Consider the shape between zero and peak. Since squaring makes small voltages even smaller relatively, will the $P$ curve look exactly like the $V$ curve or a little narrower and sharper?
parts.proper_answer: Sketch of $P$ against $t$ with rectified pulses touching zero at 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 s and peaks of 0.22 W at about 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 s, with $P$ proportional to $V^2$ shape.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use P follows V-squared**
At any instant $$P = \frac{V_{OUT}^2}{R}$$ So $P$ is zero whenever $V_{OUT}$ is zero, and maximum whenever $V_{OUT}$ is maximum. That means your $P$ graph must have minima sitting on the time axis at $t = 0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08 \text{ s}$, exactly as in Fig. 7.2.

Step 2: **Keep frequency and mark the peak**
Rectification does not change the timing, so the period of the pulses stays $0.02 \text{ s}$. Draw four identical humps in $0$ to $0.08 \text{ s}$. All maxima must reach $$P_{MAX} = 0.22 \text{ W}$$ at about $0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 \text{ s}$.

Step 3: **Get the shape right**
Because of the squaring, the curve is still like a rectified sine wave but slightly narrower and more peaked than the voltage wave. It never goes negative, and it touches zero sharply at each minimum.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: For a sinusoidal-squared variation between 0 and peak, the average over a full cycle sits halfway between zero and peak. What is half of 0.22 W?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Average a squared sine**
Since $P$ varies as $\sin^2$, its time average over each pulse is half the peak. So $$P_{mean} = \frac{P_{MAX}}{2} = \frac{0.22}{2} = 0.11 \text{ W}$$ You can also see this as half the area of a rectangle of height $0.22 \text{ W}$.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Write down what determines instantaneous heating in R. Does it depend on the sign of the voltage or only on its magnitude?
Hint 2: Compare $V^2$ at any instant for the direct sinusoidal supply with $V^2$ for the rectified supply. What does that say about the two $P$-time graphs and their averages?
parts.proper_answer: The power-time graph is identical because $P = V^2 / R$, so negative half-cycles give the same power as rectified positive half-cycles. Hence mean power is equal to 0.11 W.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Power cares about V-squared**
Heating power is $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ Squaring removes the sign. A voltage of $-9.0 \text{ V}$ gives exactly the same instantaneous $P$ as $+9.0 \text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Compare the two cases**
With R directly across the supply, $V$ across R is a full sine wave going positive and negative. With the rectifier, the negative halves are flipped positive, but after squaring the $P$ values are unchanged. So the $P$ against $t$ graph is identical in shape, peak and timing, and therefore the mean power is the same as in (b)(iii).
